content: Forkhead box protein A1 (FOXA1), also referred to as hepatocyte nuclear factor 3-alpha (HNF-3A), is a protein encoded by the FOXA1 gene in humans. FOXA1 belongs to the forkhead class of DNA-binding proteins. These proteins, known as hepatocyte nuclear factors, function as transcriptional activators for liver-specific genes, including albumin and transthyretin. Additionally, FOXA1 interacts with chromatin as a pioneer factor, facilitating the opening of chromatin to allow transcriptional machinery access to specific genomic regions. In murine models, other members of this protein family have been implicated in the regulation of metabolic processes and the differentiation of both the pancreas and liver. In the context of breast cancer, FOXA1 expression is strongly associated with the presence of ERα+ (estrogen receptor alpha-positive), GATA3+, and PR+ (progesterone receptor-positive) protein expression, as well as with endocrine signaling pathways. FOXA1 serves as a pioneer factor for ERα in ERα+ breast cancers, enabling the receptor to bind to chromatin and regulate gene expression. Its expression may also identify ERα+ breast cancers that undergo rapid reprogramming of ERα signaling, a phenomenon linked to poor clinical outcomes and resistance to treatment. On the other hand, in ERα− (estrogen receptor alpha-negative) breast cancers, FOXA1 expression is associated with low-grade tumor morphology and improved disease-free survival. Furthermore, FOXA1 is a downstream target of GATA3 in mammary gland biology. In ERα− breast cancers, FOXA1 expression may help identify a subset of tumors that could respond to alternative endocrine therapies, such as treatments targeting the androgen receptor. In prostate cancer, recurrent mutations in the FOXA1 gene have been observed, suggesting its involvement in the pathogenesis of this malignancy.
